question: Which statement best describes the relationship between a Java class and an object?

answers.text: A class is a blueprint that defines state and behavior; an object is a runtime instance of that class.
A class exists only after an object is created, while an object defines the reusable blueprint.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: This reverses the relationship. The class is the reusable blueprint, and objects are created from it at runtime.

answers.text: A class stores field values for one specific entity, while an object stores only method definitions.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Actual field values belong to objects. The class defines fields and methods, but it does not represent one specific runtime entity.

answers.text: A class and an object are interchangeable terms in Java.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: They are related but not interchangeable. A class is a definition; an object is an instance of that definition.

answerDescription: A class defines the structure and behavior that instances can have. An object is the concrete runtime instance that carries actual field values.

question: A service creates two `UserProfile` objects from the same class. Which statement is true?

answers.text: They can hold different field values even though they were created from the same class.
They must always contain identical field values because they share the same class definition.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Objects from the same class share structure and behavior, but each object has its own separate instance state.

answers.text: Only one of them can call the class methods at runtime.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Any object created from the class can call its instance methods, assuming access rules allow it.

answers.text: Creating the second object automatically replaces the first object.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Creating a new object does not replace an existing object. Both can exist independently if references to them are kept.

answerDescription: Objects created from the same class share the same structure and behavior definition, but each object has its own instance state.

question: Why is it useful to model `Order`, `Customer`, and `Invoice` as separate classes in a backend application?

answers.text: Each class can represent a distinct concept with its own state and behavior, making the model clearer and easier to maintain.
Java requires every business noun to become a class, even when no behavior or data differs.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Java does not require every noun to become a class. Classes should model useful concepts with meaningful state, behavior, or responsibility.

answers.text: Separate classes prevent objects from interacting with one another.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Objects can still interact through methods and references. Separate classes mainly improve responsibility boundaries.

answers.text: Using more classes automatically improves performance by reducing memory usage.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: More classes do not automatically improve performance or reduce memory usage. The main benefit here is clearer modeling and maintainability.

answerDescription: Classes are most useful when they give separate concepts clear responsibilities and boundaries. The benefit is maintainability and expressiveness, not automatic performance.

question: You need a class to represent a temperature reading with a numeric value and a unit, and you want callers to retrieve both pieces of data later. Which implementation is the best starting point?

answers.text: A `TemperatureReading` class with `value` and `unit` fields plus methods that expose the needed behavior.
A single `double` variable, because objects should not contain more than one piece of state.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Objects can contain multiple related pieces of state. A single `double` would lose the unit information.

answers.text: Two unrelated local variables created separately wherever a reading is needed.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Separate local variables scatter related data and make the model easier to misuse. A class keeps the value and unit together.

answers.text: A class with no fields and only a comment explaining what a reading means.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: A comment does not store runtime data. The class needs fields or behavior to represent the actual temperature reading.

answerDescription: When pieces of data belong together and describe one concept, a class is a natural way to keep that state and related behavior together.

Fields inside Java objects are always shared across every instance of the class.

question: A team stores `customerName`, `customerEmail`, `shippingStreet`, and `shippingPostalCode` directly on `Order`, even though the same customer and address concepts are reused elsewhere. Which redesign is most appropriate?

answers.text: Introduce separate `Customer` and `Address` classes and let `Order` reference them where that better matches the domain.
Move every field into static variables so all orders can reuse the same values.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Static variables would share values across all orders, which is usually incorrect for customer and address data.

answers.text: Keep adding unrelated fields to `Order` because fewer classes always make systems simpler.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Fewer classes do not automatically mean simpler design. Overloading one class with multiple concepts often makes the model harder to maintain.

answers.text: Replace all classes with primitive variables because objects are useful only for inheritance.
answers.wrongAnswerExplanation: Objects are useful for modeling related state and behavior, not only for inheritance. `Customer` and `Address` are meaningful domain concepts.

answerDescription: Classes are useful boundaries for distinct concepts. Extracting `Customer` and `Address` makes the model more expressive, reusable, and easier to evolve.
